title: GB News Doc: Ex-Google Worker Says Indians Shared Interview Questions
excerpt: Documentary alleges systematic hiring networks in Silicon Valley displaced American tech workers through H-1B visas and offshoring
body:
A former Google contractor has gone on camera to allege that Indian hiring networks in Silicon Valley systematically shared confidential interview questions to help other Indians secure positions — claims that have reignited a fierce debate over H-1B visas, offshoring, and the role of Indian-origin tech leadership in America.

**The Allegations:** Stephen Vivien, who worked as a contractor at Google, told GB News that his entire team was eliminated and their jobs sent to India, the Philippines, and Ireland. What he described as particularly galling was being asked to train his own replacements. *'It was mean, harsh, and dehumanizing,'* Vivien said. He further alleged that Indian hires would share confidential interview questions within their networks, creating what he called a dishonest pipeline of preferential hiring.

The documentary, which interviewed multiple American tech workers, also featured a former FedEx employee who spoke anonymously. She alleged that after Indian-origin CEO Raj Subramaniam took the helm, a systematic downsizing began, with her job eventually offshored to India. She claimed a manager who was ostensibly visiting family in India was actually training replacement workers.

**The Counterpoint:** Immigration attorney Navdeep Meamber, herself of Indian origin, pushed back on the narrative that Indian-origin CEOs drive preferential hiring. *'CEOs do not know who is being hired — these decisions are taken by lower-rung employees,'* she said. Meamber also noted that many Indian tech workers are voluntarily returning to India, drawn by equivalent salaries with a dramatically lower cost of living and better quality of life.

**The Policy Backdrop:** The documentary arrives at a moment of significant H-1B reform. The Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on all new H-1B entries from outside the US, though immigration expert Rosemary Jenks noted this has not reduced overall numbers because foreign students already in the country enter the workforce through the Optional Practical Training program, bypassing the new fee entirely.

**Why It Matters to the Diaspora:** For Indian Americans in tech — many of whom arrived on H-1B visas themselves — the documentary is deeply uncomfortable. It conflates individual bad actors with an entire community, feeding nativist narratives at a time when anti-immigrant sentiment is already elevated. Yet the underlying questions about workforce displacement, corporate offshoring incentives, and hiring transparency deserve honest examination rather than reflexive defensiveness.

**What to watch:** The H-1B public comment period closes May 26. Whatever rules emerge will shape hiring dynamics for the next generation of Indian tech workers seeking to build careers in America.
nri_angle: Indian Americans in tech face uncomfortable scrutiny as documentary conflates individual allegations with community-wide hiring practices amid H-1B reform
author: Diaspora Desk
